title: Jaishankar Says India-US Trade Deal Is Near the 'Finishing Line'
excerpt: The external affairs minister told the HT Leadership Summit that the bulk of issues, including tariff lines, are resolved — and that most of what remains sits on the American side.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said on Saturday that India-US trade negotiations are approaching the "finishing line," with the bulk of issues — including tariff lines — sorted out.
  • The remaining concerns are "not so much at our end," he said, because more of the changes in the talks have occurred on the American side.
  • India wants a deal that is beneficial, balanced and gives it a comparative advantage over comparable economies; the US is India's biggest market.
  • Attention now turns to the G20 Summit in Miami on December 14–15, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump may meet and speculation has centred on a first-tranche announcement.

India and the United States have sorted out the bulk of the issues in their proposed trade deal, including tariff lines, and the agreement could be sealed "soon," External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said on Saturday at the HT Leadership Summit in New Delhi. In an interactive session at the summit, he said the negotiations are approaching the "finishing line" and that many of the remaining issues are "not so much at our end," because the changes have been more at the American end than India's.

"If you are serious, you go tariff line by tariff line. That takes time. Now we've done it the painstaking way."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

What has been resolved

"Well, it's certainly our hope, and in many ways anticipation that we are at the last stretch. That's not a secret," Jaishankar said. "The hope is that we should close it out soon. It's always the case that in that last period, everybody's impatient." He said his understanding was that the bulk of the issues were sorted out, and he suggested that issues relating to tariffs were among those resolved. "For us the key is that we want a trade deal which is beneficial, it is balanced and which would give us a comparative advantage over groups of comparable economies," he said. "That is really what we are looking for and that is really our expectation of where we would be when the trade deal is done."

What is still holding it up

The Times of India reported that Jaishankar's comments may indicate the government is awaiting the next step from the Trump administration. A team of US officials came to India a week ago to discuss the customs and trade facilitation chapter, while India waits for clarity on what the new tariff framework will be after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's "reciprocal tariffs" were illegal. Movement on the deal, the report said, can come only after the US Trade Representative completes a second Section 301 probe against over a dozen countries for structural overcapacity. Washington has separately assured India a comparative tariff advantage over rival economies under the pact, as we reported earlier today in our coverage of the first tranche taking shape — though officials have cautioned that the advantage depends on how the final tariff framework unfolds.

Why this deal, and why it has taken so long

India and the US have been in talks since early 2025 on the proposed pact, which aims to address tariff friction, eliminate non-tariff barriers and boost bilateral market access. Jaishankar said the US is India's biggest market and the world's largest economy, so a trade deal with it would benefit India; for the US, he said, Trump is looking to conclude a set of bilateral deals, and "the challenge is to find a landing point." He resisted the idea that the agreement could have been concluded quickly: "I think this is not something which could have been done quickly and magically... because these are very serious issues, people's jobs and people's lives are at stake."

The talks carry the weight of a difficult year in the relationship. India-US ties went through a major downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year, and were strained further by Washington's new immigration policy and its decision to increase the H-1B visa fee, The Hindu BusinessLine noted. Last month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Mumbai that both sides were very close to firming up the trade deal.

What happens next

Jaishankar's remarks come a month before Prime Minister Narendra Modi's likely visit to the US for the G20 Summit in Miami on December 14 and 15, on the sidelines of which he and President Trump may meet to review bilateral ties and progress on the pact. There has been speculation that the two sides may announce the deal following those talks. If the trade deal is finalised, it could trigger an upswing in the overall trajectory of India-US relations. For Indian exporters and the diaspora businesses that trade between the two countries, the operative questions remain the ones Jaishankar left open: the final tariff lines, and whether the first tranche lands at the G20 or slips into the new year.
